title: "Contact Rules and Penalties as Strategy"
subtitle: "Why the same grab costs five yards before the throw and forty after it, why linemen hold, and how a yellow flag rewrites a series"
description: "The NFL's contact rules read as a price list: the five-yard contact zone, illegal contact and defensive holding, defensive and offensive pass interference (the spot foul, throwing deep to draw it, and the one-yard limit on pick plays), offensive holding and hands to the face, blocks in the back, cut and chop blocks, the player-safety rules (roughing the passer, the sliding quarterback, the defenseless player, the 2018 helmet rule, the horse-collar and hip-drop bans, the 2026 three-strike policy), how a flag is enforced (accept or decline, free plays, half the distance), what penalties cost in expected points, and the rule debates still open."
glossary:
  "Illegal contact": "A defender initiating contact that impedes a receiver more than five yards past the line of scrimmage before the pass is thrown, while the quarterback is still in the pocket with the ball. Five yards and an automatic first down."
  "Defensive holding": "A defender grabbing, hooking or otherwise restricting an eligible receiver (or any offensive player who is not the ball carrier) before a pass is thrown. Five yards and an automatic first down."
  "Offensive holding": "A blocker using his hands or arms to materially restrict a defender: grabbing, hooking, turning or tackling him, or pulling him to the ground, whether his hands are inside or outside the defender's frame. Ten yards, and a safety if it happens in the offense's own end zone."
  "Defensive pass interference": {def: "Contact by a defender, after the ball is thrown and more than one yard past the line of scrimmage, that significantly hinders a receiver's chance to catch a catchable pass. In the NFL it is a spot foul: an automatic first down at the spot of the foul, or at the 1-yard line if the foul is in the end zone.", aliases: ["DPI"]}
  "Offensive pass interference": {def: "Contact by an offensive player more than one yard past the line of scrimmage, from the snap until the pass is touched, that hinders a defender: pushing off for separation, or blocking a defender downfield before the pass (an illegal pick). Ten yards from the previous spot.", aliases: ["OPI"]}
  "Spot foul": "A foul enforced from the spot where it happened rather than from where the ball was snapped. In the NFL the famous one is defensive pass interference, which puts the ball where the foul occurred."
  "Illegal hands to the face": "Pushing, punching or grabbing an opponent's face mask, helmet or neck area with the hands, by a blocker or a defender (the stat sheet calls it illegal use of hands). Ten yards against the offense; five yards and an automatic first down against the defense."
  "Block in the back": "Pushing or blocking an opponent from behind above the waist when he is not the ball carrier. The NFL's name for it is an illegal block above the waist; ten yards. The same block below the waist is clipping, fifteen yards."
  "Chop block": "Two blockers taking on the same defender, one high and one low at the thigh or below, together or one right after the other. Banned in every situation in the NFL since 2016; fifteen yards."
  "Roughing the passer": "An unnecessary or dangerous hit on a quarterback who is passing or has just thrown: a hit after the ball is clearly gone, forcible contact to his head or neck, a hit at or below the knees, or landing on him with all or most of the defender's body weight. Fifteen yards and an automatic first down."
  "Unnecessary roughness": "The catch-all personal foul for needless or dangerous contact: late hits after the whistle, hits on a player out of bounds, forcible hits on a defenseless player, and the like. Fifteen yards, plus an automatic first down when the defense commits it."
  "Defenseless player": "A player the rules treat as unable to protect himself (a passer throwing, a receiver trying to catch a pass, a player on the ground, a kicker or returner during the kick, and others) and so protect from forcible hits to the head and neck and from launching."
  "Use of the helmet (2018 rule)": "The NFL rule, adopted in 2018, that makes it a foul for any player anywhere on the field to lower his head to initiate and make contact with his helmet against an opponent. Fifteen yards, and the player may be ejected."
  "Horse-collar tackle": "Grabbing the inside back or side collar of a ball carrier's shoulder pads or jersey and pulling him down. Banned in the NFL since 2005; fifteen yards."
  "Hip-drop tackle": "A tackle in which the tackler wraps the runner from behind or the side, swings his hips and legs off the ground, and drops his weight onto the runner's legs at or below the knee. Banned by the NFL in 2024; fifteen yards and an automatic first down."
  "Free play": "A snap on which the defense has already committed a foul that lets play go on (usually offside), so the offense can take a risk knowing it may either keep the result or take the penalty instead."
  "Accept / decline (penalty)": "The fouled team's choice after a foul during a play: accept the penalty (the play's result is usually wiped out and the yardage enforced) or decline it and keep the result of the play as though no foul had happened."
  "Half the distance": "The cap on penalty yardage near a goal line: when the full penalty would move the ball more than halfway to the offending team's goal line, the ball moves only halfway instead."

import os
import logging
import textwrap

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch, Polygon, Circle, Ellipse
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from IPython.display import Markdown

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, defense, routes as r, show_animation, style, draw_marker

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")

LEGAL = "#0f7a55"       # dark green: legal contact
LEGAL_T = "#d7efe4"
FOUL = "#b8321f"        # dark red: a foul
FOUL_T = "#fbe1da"
FLAG_Y = "#f2c200"      # the yellow flag
FIELD_W = 160 / 3


def P_(fld, p, d, w):
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    return float(x), float(y)


def no_numbers(ax):
    """Remove gridiron's painted yard-line numbers (they sit where receivers stand)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK, fs=6.8, ha="center", weight="normal", box=True, style_="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w), on a pale backing so lines under it stay out of the way."""
    x, y = P_(fld, p, d, w)
    kw = dict(bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.93)) if box else {}
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fs, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=12, fontweight=weight,
                linespacing=1.12, style=style_, **kw)


def band(fld, p, d0, d1, color, alpha=1.0, w0=-26.7, w1=26.7, z=0.6):
    """Shade the strip of field between depths d0 and d1."""
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = P_(fld, p, d0, w0), P_(fld, p, d1, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(xa, xb), min(ya, yb)), abs(xb - xa), abs(yb - ya), fc=color,
                               alpha=alpha, ec="none", zorder=z))


def line_across(fld, p, d, color, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (4, 2)), w0=-26.7, w1=26.7, z=2.5):
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = P_(fld, p, d, w0), P_(fld, p, d, w1)
    fld.ax.plot([xa, xb], [ya, yb], color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=z)


def star(fld, p, d, w, color, ms=12):
    """Where the contact happens."""
    x, y = P_(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.plot([x], [y], marker="*", ms=ms, color=color, mec="white", mew=0.7, zorder=13)


def flag(fld, p, d, w, s=1.0):
    """A small yellow penalty flag planted at (d, w); drawn in plot yards, so it stands upright in either view."""
    x, y = P_(fld, p, d, w)
    ax = fld.ax
    ax.plot([x, x], [y, y + 1.9 * s], color=style.INK, lw=0.9, zorder=14, solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.add_patch(Polygon([(x, y + 1.9 * s), (x + 1.5 * s, y + 1.5 * s), (x, y + 1.05 * s)], closed=True,
                         fc=FLAG_Y, ec=style.INK, lw=0.5, zorder=14))


def ball(fld, p, d, w, z=13):
    x, y = P_(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y), 1.3, 0.8, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.7, zorder=z))


def arrow(fld, p, frm, to, color, lw=1.6, z=5, ls="-", ms=10, rad=0.0):
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(P_(fld, p, *frm), P_(fld, p, *to), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=ms,
                                     color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=z, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0,
                                     connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}"))


def trail(fld, p, pts, color, lw=1.1, ls=(0, (1, 1.6)), alpha=0.9, z=3):
    xs, ys = zip(*[P_(fld, p, d, w) for d, w in pts])
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, alpha=alpha, zorder=z)


def panel_title(ax, text, fs=8.5):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=fs, color=style.INK, loc="left", fontweight="bold")


def O_(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D_(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line5():
    """Five offensive linemen on the ball (gridiron's spacing), labels off."""
    return [O_(k, k, -0.7, w, "C" if k == "C" else "") for k, w in
            (("LT", -3.2), ("LG", -1.6), ("C", 0.0), ("RG", 1.6), ("RT", 3.2))]


# ------------------------------------------------- the print version of an animation
def snapshot(play, t, ax, lateral, window, notes=(), flags=(), stars=()):
    """Everyone where he is at time t, with faint trails of where the skill players have been."""
    pos = {k: play.position(k, t) for k in play.players}
    moved = [pl.moved(d=float(pos[k][0]), w=float(pos[k][1])) for k, pl in play.players.items()]
    q = Play([m for m in moved if m.side == "off"], [m for m in moved if m.side == "def"],
             los=play.los, ball_y=play.ball_y, to_go=play.to_go)
    q.highlights = dict(play.highlights)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, title=False)
    no_numbers(fld.ax)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    t0 = play._compile()[1]
    for k, pl in play.players.items():
        if pl.side == "off" and pl.pos not in ("WR", "TE", "RB"):
            continue
        if pl.side == "def" and pl.pos in ("DE", "DT", "NT"):
            continue
        pts = np.array([play.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(t0, t, 40)])
        if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.3:
            continue
        xs, ys = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1]))
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if pl.side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, alpha=0.5, zorder=3)
    bx, by = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*play.ball_position(t)))
    for kind, _, t_rel in play.ball_events:
        if kind == "pass" and t > t_rel:
            sx, sy = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*play.ball_position(t_rel)))
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(sx), float(sy)), (float(bx), float(by)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=8, color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9))
    draw_marker(ax, float(bx), float(by), "ball", "", ppy)
    for d, w in flags:
        flag(fld, q, d, w)
    for d, w, c in stars:
        star(fld, q, d, w, c)
    for n in notes:
        d, w, text = n[:3]
        kw = n[3] if len(n) > 3 else {}
        say(fld, q, d, w, text, **kw)
    for txt in ax.texts:                       # labels of players outside the window stay out of sight
        txt.set_clip_on(True)
    return fld


def strip(play, times, labels, lateral, window, per_panel=None, width_in=6.5, ncols=2):
    """Panels at chosen moments; per_panel[i] = dict(notes=..., flags=..., stars=...)."""
    n = len(times)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    h = nrows * (pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]) + 0.34)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, h), squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t, lab) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times, labels)):
        extra = (per_panel or {}).get(i, {})
        snapshot(play, t, ax, lateral, window, **extra)
        panel_title(ax, lab, fs=8.3)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.7, w_pad=0.5)
    return fig

from gridiron.data import pbp

COLS = ["season", "season_type", "week", "game_id", "play_id", "play_type", "desc", "posteam", "defteam",
        "penalty", "penalty_type", "penalty_team", "penalty_yards", "first_down_penalty", "epa", "down",
        "ydstogo", "yardline_100", "pass", "rush", "pass_attempt", "pass_length", "sack", "complete_pass",
        "interception", "first_down", "touchdown"]
PB = pbp(range(2015, 2026), columns=COLS)
REG = PB[PB.season_type == "REG"].copy()
REG["declined"] = REG.desc.str.contains("declined", case=False, na=False)
GAMES = REG.groupby("season").game_id.nunique()

# Flags as nflverse files them: one penalty type per play (the play's main foul), accepted or declined,
# on every kind of play (kicks included).
FLAG = REG[REG.penalty == 1]
RATES = FLAG.groupby(["season", "penalty_type"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0).div(GAMES, axis=0)
ALL_FLAGS = REG.desc.str.count("PENALTY on").groupby(REG.season).sum().div(GAMES)   # every foul named

# Accepted fouls on scrimmage downs, 2021-2025: what each kind of flag is worth in expected points.
KICKS = ["kickoff", "punt", "field_goal", "extra_point"]
REC = FLAG[(FLAG.season >= 2021) & ~FLAG.declined & FLAG.down.notna() & ~FLAG.play_type.isin(KICKS)].copy()
REC["by_off"] = REC.penalty_team == REC.posteam
EPA_T = REC.groupby("penalty_type").agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"), yds=("penalty_yards", "mean"),
                                        fd=("first_down_penalty", "mean"), by_off=("by_off", "mean"))
EPA_S = REC.groupby(["penalty_type", "by_off"]).agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"),
                                                 yds=("penalty_yards", "mean"))   # split by the side that fouled

# Defensive pass interference: how far, how often, short throws against deep ones (15+ air yards).
DPI = REC[REC.penalty_type == "Defensive Pass Interference"].copy()
DPI["depth"] = np.select([DPI.desc.str.contains(r"pass (?:incomplete |complete )?deep", regex=True),
                          DPI.desc.str.contains(r"pass (?:incomplete |complete )?short", regex=True)],
                         ["deep", "short"], "")
THROWS = REG[(REG.season >= 2021) & (REG.pass_attempt == 1) & (REG.sack != 1) & (REG.play_type == "pass")
             & REG.pass_length.notna()]
N_THROW = THROWS.pass_length.value_counts()
N_DPI = DPI.depth.value_counts()
DPI_RATE = {k: 100 * N_DPI.get(k, 0) / (N_THROW[k] + N_DPI.get(k, 0)) for k in ("short", "deep")}
DPI_YDS = DPI.groupby("depth").penalty_yards.mean()
DEEP_EPA = THROWS[THROWS.pass_length == "deep"].epa.mean()
DEEP_EPA_DPI = pd.concat([THROWS[THROWS.pass_length == "deep"].epa, DPI[DPI.depth == "deep"].epa]).mean()
OVER15 = (DPI.penalty_yards > 15).mean()
OVER30 = (DPI.penalty_yards >= 30).mean()
COMP_EPA = THROWS[THROWS.complete_pass == 1].epa.mean()
SACK_EPA = REG[(REG.season >= 2021) & (REG.sack == 1) & REG.down.notna()].epa.mean()

# The same five-yard defensive fouls, down by down.
BYDOWN = (REC[REC.penalty_type.isin(["Defensive Holding", "Illegal Contact"])]
          .groupby("down").agg(n=("epa", "size"), togo=("ydstogo", "mean"), epa=("epa", "mean")))

# Third-and-long: how often a third down with 16-20 to go is converted (first down or touchdown).
SCRIM = REG[(REG.season >= 2021) & REG.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"]) & REG.down.notna()]
T3L = SCRIM[(SCRIM.down == 3) & SCRIM.ydstogo.between(16, 20)]
CONV_3L = ((T3L.first_down == 1) | (T3L.touchdown == 1)).mean()
T38 = SCRIM[(SCRIM.down == 3) & (SCRIM.ydstogo == 8)]
CONV_38 = ((T38.first_down == 1) | (T38.touchdown == 1)).mean()

HIP = FLAG[FLAG.penalty_type == "Hip Drop Tackle"].groupby("season").size()

    rows = [list(df.columns), ["---:" if i else ":---" for i in range(len(df.columns))]] + df.astype(str).values.tolist()

Third-and-9, a minute left in the half. The quarterback takes a deep drop and heaves the ball 45
yards down the left sideline toward a receiver who is not open. The cornerback is with him stride for
stride, the ball comes down a yard out of reach, and the crowd groans. Then a yellow flag lands on
the grass. The corner had grabbed the receiver's arm a split second before the ball arrived. Pass
interference: first down, at the spot of the foul. A throw that was going nowhere has just gained 41
yards, and the rules analyst in the booth says the offense "knew exactly what it was doing." Two
questions hide in that sentence. Why would a coach call a throw he expects to be incomplete? And why
is the same grab worth five yards if it happens one second earlier, before the ball is in the air?
This chapter reads the rule book the way coaches do: as a list of prices.

**You'll be able to…**

- Say where a defender may touch a receiver and when (the five-yard zone, then hands off until the
  throw, then the pass-interference rules) and name the foul for each kind of contact.
- Explain why defensive pass interference is a spot foul in the NFL and a 15-yard foul in college,
  and why that one difference makes NFL offenses throw deep into tight coverage.
- Tell a legal rub from an illegal pick by where the contact happens, and explain what holding,
  hands to the face, blocks in the back, cut blocks and chop blocks cost.
- Explain the player-safety rules (roughing the passer, the sliding quarterback, the defenseless
  player, the 2018 helmet rule, the horse-collar and hip-drop bans, the 2026 three-strike policy) and
  why each was written.
- Enforce a flag yourself: accept or decline, from which spot, how far (including half the
  distance), and what down it is next. Then call the foul before the referee announces it.
- Read a chart of penalty rates and say how a flag enters expected points (EPA).

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
This chapter leans on a few earlier ones. One line each:

- **Press and the five-yard rule** ([Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)):
  a [press](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-press) corner lines up in the receiver's face to jam
  him at the snap; defenders may touch receivers only in the first five yards, a limit dating to the
  1978 "Mel Blount rule." [Man coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-coverage) gives each
  defender a receiver; [zone coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-coverage) gives each an
  area.
- **Pass protection** ([Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd)): five
  linemen (and sometimes backs and tight ends) block four or more rushers so the quarterback can throw
  from the [pocket](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pocket), the protected area behind the line.
  A [sack](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sack) is the quarterback tackled behind the line.
- **The one-yard rule for linemen** ([Run-Pass Options](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd)): on a
  pass, an ineligible lineman may not be more than a yard downfield before the ball is thrown, the foul
  called [illegal man downfield](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-illegal-man-downfield). It is why NFL
  RPOs look the way they do.
- **Rub routes** ([Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)): a
  [rub route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rub-route) (also
  [pick route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pick-route)) crosses receivers so a defender
  chasing one runs into traffic.
- **Cut blocks** ([Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd)): a
  [cut block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cut-block) is a block at a defender's thighs or below,
  from the front, to put him on the ground. Two words from
  [The Language of the Run Game](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd) come back here: a
  [3-technique](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3-technique) is a defensive tackle lined up on a
  guard's outside shoulder, and the *backside* is the side away from where the run is going.
- **Pre-snap fouls** ([The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)): a
  [false start](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-false-start) or
  [encroachment](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-encroachment) stops the play before it starts;
  [offside](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-offside) lets it run. A foul that lets the play run is a
  *live-ball foul*, and the ball's spot before the snap is the *previous spot*.
- **Expected points** ([Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)):
  [expected points](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-expected-points) price a down, distance and yard
  line; [EPA](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa) is the change in that price over one play. The
  [line to gain](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-the-sticks) is "the sticks."

*Reading the diagrams:* offense is blue circles (X, Y, Z, H receivers; Q quarterback; R running
back; C center; unlabelled circles are linemen). Defense is outlined squares (C a cornerback, $ the
nickel back, FS the free safety, E and T linemen, M and W linebackers). Players with a **green
ring** are the ones to watch. The darker blue line is the line of scrimmage and the faint lines are
5 yards apart. In this chapter a **star** marks a moment of contact (green: legal; red: a foul) and a
yellow **flag** marks where an official would throw one.

## The rule book as a price list

Every sport has rules about contact. Football has more of them than most, because almost every
player on almost every snap is allowed to hit somebody. The rules don't try to stop contact. They
decide **who may touch whom, where, and when**, and they attach a price to each violation: five
yards, ten, fifteen, a first down, the spot of the foul, a safety, an ejection.

Prices change behaviour. A cornerback knows that grabbing a receiver before the throw costs five
yards *and an automatic first down*. On third-and-20 that price is ruinous: the defense was one
incompletion away from a punt, and the grab hands the offense a fresh set of downs. On first-and-10,
with the receiver running past him for a touchdown, the same grab is a bargain. An offensive lineman beaten by a pass rusher will often hold rather than let his quarterback
be sacked, because ten yards cost less than a sack plus the chance of a fumble. A play-caller who
knows that pass interference is enforced at the spot will throw deep into coverage, because the
flag is one of the throw's possible outcomes. None of this is cheating; it's arithmetic. Coaches
teach it, and the NFL's competition committee, which proposes the rule changes the owners vote on
each spring, adjusts the prices when it doesn't like how teams respond.

This chapter takes the rules in four groups:

1. **Contact on receivers**, the rules that shape pass coverage and route design: illegal contact,
   defensive holding, and pass interference in both directions.
2. **Blocking rules**, which shape what linemen and receivers may do: holding, hands to the face,
   blocks in the back, cut and chop blocks, and the lineman's one-yard limit on passes.
3. **Player-safety rules**, mostly written in the last twenty years to protect heads, knees and
   quarterbacks.
4. **Enforcement**, the mechanics that turn a flag into a new down and distance: accepting and
   declining, free plays, where the yards are walked off, and half the distance.

Then we price them with data: how often each foul is called, and what it does to expected points.
(Officials, replay review and the rules of the ball itself, what counts as a catch or a fumble, are
the next chapter, [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd).)

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Football's contact rules exist to keep two contests fair at once. One is between the offense and
the defense: without limits, defenders would tackle receivers before every pass and linemen would
tackle pass rushers, and the passing game would die. The other is between the players and the
damage they can do to each other. Most rule changes of the last half-century have pushed one or both
of those two ways: toward offense (1978, 2004) and toward safety (2005 onward). Read any rule
change by asking which contest it was protecting.
:::

## The receiver's first five yards: illegal contact and defensive holding

A pass play is a race. The receiver needs to reach a spot on the field at a set time, and the
quarterback needs to throw it there before the rush arrives. A defender's best weapon in that race
is his hands: knock the receiver off his line, slow him, turn him, and the timing of the whole play
breaks. The NFL rules allow exactly a little of that.

Here are the rules, as the NFL writes them for 2026:[^contact-rule]

- **Within five yards of the line of scrimmage**, a defender may *chuck* (jam, push, re-route) a
  receiver who is in front of him. That is what a press corner is doing at the snap.
- **Beyond five yards**, while the quarterback is still in the pocket with the ball, a defender may
  not initiate contact with the receiver. He may use his hands only to protect himself, and contact
  that started inside the five yards has to end as the two of them leave the zone: he may not shove,
  hook or ride him past it. The foul is
  [**illegal contact**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-illegal-contact): **five yards and an
  automatic first down**.
- **Anywhere on the field**, before the pass is thrown, a defender may not grab, hook or tackle a
  receiver, or otherwise restrict him: **[defensive holding](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-defensive-holding)**,
  also **five yards and an automatic first down**. Holding can happen inside the five yards too. A
  jam with open hands is legal; a fistful of jersey is not.
- **Once the ball is thrown**, both of those rules hand over to the pass-interference rules, below.
- The illegal-contact restriction lifts when the quarterback **leaves the pocket**, so on a scramble
  a defender may chuck a receiver beyond five yards. Holding is still holding, and once the ball is in
  the air pass interference applies again. "The pocket" here has an exact meaning: the rule book's
  *pocket area* runs between where the two tackles lined up, from the line back to the offense's end
  line, and the quarterback has left it once any part of him or the ball is outside it.
  [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd)
  draws it as the [tackle box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tackle-box).[^pocket]

Defensive holding isn't only about receivers. The rule bans a defender holding *any* offensive
player other than the ball carrier, and the version you'll see flagged most at the line is a
defensive lineman grabbing a blocker on a [stunt](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stunt) (a
pass-rush game in which rushers cross), pinning a guard so the looping teammate can come free
([The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd)). Same price: five yards and
an automatic first down.

Two prices, five yards and a first down, look small next to pass interference, and they are meant
to. The automatic first down is the expensive part. On first-and-10 a five-yard foul gives the
offense first-and-5, a nice gain. On third-and-12 it erases the down: the defense had the offense
behind the sticks and needed one stop, and now it starts the series over. (The numbers on this,
down by down, are in [What penalties cost](#what-penalties-cost), below.)

### Why five yards, and the year it started to bite

[Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) told the origin: the
five-yard zone dates from the 1978 "Mel Blount rule," the same package that let offensive linemen
extend their arms and open their hands in pass protection, and both halves pointed toward
passing.[^blount] ([The 1978 Liberation](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd) tells that
story in full.) What matters here is what came next. The rule sat on the books for 25 years
without being enforced very hard. Defensive backs learned what officials would tolerate (a hand on
the hip at eight yards, a tug at the top of the route), and by the early 2000s the best press teams
were playing the 1977 game with 1978 rules. This film room is the game that ended that.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Patriots vs. Colts, 2003 AFC Championship (Jan. 18, 2004)"}
In the AFC Championship Game after the 2003 season, Bill Belichick's Patriots beat Peyton
Manning's Colts 24–14 in Foxborough. Manning, that season's co-MVP, threw four
interceptions, three of them to cornerback Ty Law.[^afc2003] On the film, New England's defensive
backs jam, ride and bump Indianapolis's receivers well past five yards, all game, and few flags fly.

The Colts' president, Bill Polian, sat on the competition committee. That off-season the committee
made illegal contact and defensive holding beyond five yards a "point of emphasis": officials were
told to call the rule as written. Patriots fans call it the "Ty Law rule." The flags came at once: by
one count illegal-contact fouls rose from 79 in the 2003 regular season to 191 in 2004
(nflverse's play-by-play, which records only one foul per play, has 49 and 123), and teams averaged
about 225 passing yards a game in 2004, up from 214.[^tylaw] Manning threw 49 touchdown passes in
2004, breaking Dan Marino's single-season record.[^manning]

**What to notice:** the rule didn't change; its price did. A rule that is called is a different rule
from one that isn't, which is why "points of emphasis" announced each summer are worth reading. On
a broadcast, watch a press corner's hands after the receiver's fifth step. If they stay on him, the
next flag is coming.
:::

### What the five-yard zone does to schemes

[Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) covered what the zone
does to press (all of the jam has to land in about the first second, so pressed corners want a
safety behind them) and to releases (stacks, bunches and motion that dodge the jam). Three more
effects:

- **Zone defenders have to pass receivers off, not re-route them.** A linebacker in a hook zone
  may not shove a crossing receiver at eight yards, so zone defense is about positioning, not
  collision. The jam that survives is the Cover 2 corner's, which happens inside the five yards
  ([Cover 2 and Tampa 2](../06-pass-coverage/06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd)).
- **A scramble changes the rules.** When the quarterback leaves the pocket, defenders may chuck
  receivers downfield again. Part of why the scramble drill
  ([Quarterback Play](../04-the-passing-game/04-07-quarterback-play.qmd)) is hard to defend is that
  coverage gets messy; part of why it is not easier is that defenders get their hands back.
- **Smart fouls.** A corner beaten off the line on a go route can grab the receiver before the throw
  and give up five yards and a first down rather than a touchdown. Nobody coaches it out loud, but
  everybody knows the price.

## Pass interference, both ways

Once the ball is thrown, the question changes from "may he touch the receiver?" to "is he
playing the ball?" **[Defensive pass interference](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-defensive-pass-interference)**
([**DPI**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dpi)) is contact by a defender, after the ball is thrown
and more than one yard past the line of scrimmage, that **significantly hinders** an eligible
receiver's chance to catch the ball. The rule lists the usual acts: grabbing an arm or the jersey,
cutting in front of the receiver without looking for the ball, hooking him, putting an arm across his
body, tackling him early. And it lists what is *not* interference:[^pi-rule]

- contact when both players are making a genuine attempt to catch or bat the ball;
- incidental contact, such as feet tangling, that doesn't materially affect the receiver;
- contact on a pass that is **clearly uncatchable**;
- contact before the throw, which is illegal contact or holding instead (five yards), not DPI.

**[Offensive pass interference](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-offensive-pass-interference)**
([**OPI**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-opi)) is the mirror image, with one big difference:
the offense's restrictions start at the **snap**, not the throw. From the snap until the pass is
touched, an offensive player more than a yard past the line may not initiate contact that hinders a
defender. The two everyday versions are the **push-off** (a receiver extends his arm to create
separation at the top of a route or at the catch point) and the **illegal pick** (a receiver blocks
a defender downfield before the ball is thrown, to free a teammate). OPI costs **ten yards from the
previous spot**, and the down is replayed.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"He grabbed the receiver, so it's pass interference." Only if the ball was in the air. The same
grab a second before the throw is defensive holding (five yards and a first down); a hard shove at
eight yards before the throw is illegal contact (same price). The difference matters enormously,
because DPI is enforced at the spot. When a flag flies on a pass, look at whether the ball had left
the quarterback's hand at the moment of the foul, and you'll know which of the three it is.
:::

### The one-yard strip, and who started the contact

[Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) introduced rub routes and
warned that they can become illegal picks. Here is the rule that draws the line. Pass interference
by either side can only happen **more than one yard past the line of scrimmage**.[^rub-rule] Two
tests follow from that, one about *where* and one about *who*:

- **Inside the first yard, even a deliberate pick is legal.** A receiver may release straight into
  the defender covering a teammate, and if the bump happens within a yard of the line there is no
  interference (a grab there can still be holding).
- **Beyond the first yard, the question is who initiated the contact.** OPI needs the offensive
  player to *do* something: push off, or block or obstruct a defender before the ball is touched. A
  receiver who keeps running his route while a defender chasing someone else has to go around him,
  or runs into him, hasn't fouled at any depth. That is the *natural rub*, and it is how
  [mesh](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mesh) and other crossing concepts free receivers 5 or 6
  yards downfield every week. If the receiver stops, turns his shoulders to the defender or extends
  his arms, he has started a block, and it's OPI.

Offenses coach the legal versions: make the contact happen at the line, or keep running the route
and let the defender run into you. Officials, judging at full speed, look for the giveaways of a
block (a receiver who stops, turns his shoulders or extends his arms). Stacks and bunches
([Spread Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)) put
receivers' paths across defenders in the first step or two, where the strip makes it legal.

Defenses answer in three ways. They play **zone** against bunches, because a zone defender isn't
chasing anyone through traffic. They **switch** (or *banjo*) in man coverage, trading receivers by
agreement so nobody has to chase through the cross ([Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd)).
And they **align deeper**: a defender who lines up four or five yards off the ball can't be picked
inside the first yard, because he's not there yet, and has room to go over or under a crosser.
When the officials do see a pick, it is OPI: **ten yards from the previous spot**, the down
replayed, and any completion wiped out.

### The spot foul: why DPI is football's most expensive flag

Most fouls are enforced from the **previous spot**, where the ball was snapped. Defensive pass
interference is different. In the NFL it is a
**[spot foul](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spot-foul)**: the offense gets an automatic first
down **at the spot where the foul happened**, however far downfield that is. A foul 40 yards past the
line is a 40-yard penalty. If the foul happens in the end zone, the ball goes to the **1-yard line**,
first and goal.[^dpi-enf]

College football does it differently. Under the NCAA rule, defensive pass interference is **15
yards from the previous spot** and an automatic first down; only when the foul happens less than 15
yards downfield is it enforced at the spot.[^college-dpi] The high-school rule is also 15 yards. The
NFL is the outlier, and it is the reason the most consequential judgment call in football carries
no cap.

::: {#cell-fig-dpi-enforcement .cell execution_count=5}

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: the spot foul"}
**What it solves.** The NFL's logic is that a penalty should give back what the foul took away. A
defender beaten deep who tackles the receiver before the ball arrives has prevented, quite
possibly, a 40-yard completion. Cap the penalty at 15 yards and every beaten defender would happily
pay it. With no cap, there's nothing to gain by tackling a receiver who has beaten you; you have to
play the ball.

**What it costs.** The penalty is huge and the call is a judgment. "Significantly hinders" is
decided at full speed by an official who may be 20 yards away, and the difference between a
legal, hand-fighting 50-50 ball and a 45-yard flag is sometimes a single tug. That combination makes
DPI the call most likely to decide a game, and it is why fans and coaches keep proposing either the
college cap or replay review for it. (The NFL tried replay once; see the film room below.)
:::

### What the spot foul does to offenses: throw deep, into coverage

Put the two rules together and an NFL offense has a reason to throw deep that a college offense
doesn't. Each deep pass has four kinds of outcome: a completion, an incompletion, an interception,
and a defensive pass interference flag, which is, in effect, a long completion that also stops the
clock. In the 2021–2025 regular seasons, throws travelling 15 or more yards in the air drew a DPI
flag about 4\.1 times per 100 throws, against about
0\.9 for shorter ones, and those deep flags averaged
23 yards. Counting them in raises the expected points of an average
deep throw from \+0\.38 to \+0\.45 per attempt.[^data-dpi]

::: {#cell-fig-deep-dpi .cell execution_count=6}

That's why you see things that look like bad decisions: a quarterback throwing up a 50-50 ball to a
receiver who is covered, or a [back-shoulder throw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-back-shoulder-throw)
(a ball thrown behind a receiver's outside shoulder, so he turns back for it while the defender is
still running) into a corner who has his back turned. Two of the
outcomes (a catch or a flag) are big gains, one (an incompletion) costs a down, and only the
interception is a disaster. Big, physical receivers are worth more in the NFL partly because they
win those balls *or* draw the flag, and defensive backs are taught to turn and find the ball, because
a defender who never looks back isn't "playing the ball" and any contact gets flagged
([Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd)).

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Rams at Saints, 2018 NFC Championship (Jan. 20, 2019)"}
Late in the fourth quarter, the score tied at 20, New Orleans had third-and-10 at the Rams' 13 with
about 1:49 to play. Drew Brees threw to Tommylee Lewis near the right sideline, and Rams cornerback
Nickell Robey-Coleman, who later said he had been beaten, hit Lewis well before the ball arrived,
helmet to helmet. No flag. A flag would have meant a first down inside the 10, and with the Rams
down to one timeout the Saints could have run the clock to about ten seconds before kicking. Instead
they kicked a field goal on fourth down with 1:41 left, the Rams tied it, and they won 26–23 in
overtime.[^nfc2018]

The league admitted the call was missed. Two months later the owners approved a one-year
experiment: pass interference, called or not, became **reviewable by replay**, by
[coach's challenge](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-coach-s-challenge) or, in the last two minutes
and overtime, by [booth review](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-booth-review). It was a mess. Replay officials, reluctant to
re-referee a judgment call, overturned very few calls or no-calls, coaches stopped challenging, and
the rule was allowed to lapse after the 2019 season.[^pireview]

**What to notice:** the NFL's experience is why "just review it" isn't simple. Replay works for
facts (was his foot down? where was the ball?) and struggles with degree (did he *significantly*
hinder him?). Since 2025 [replay assist](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-replay-assist) may help on
a short list of fouls, but pass interference is not among them; [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd)
covers what replay can and can't do now.
:::

## Blocking rules: holding, hands to the face, and where a block may land

Offensive holding is, in most seasons, the most-called foul in the NFL (false starts edged it in
2020 and 2023), and also the one that, by common agreement,
officials could call on nearly every snap. Blocking means leverage and hands. The line between
blocking a defender and holding him is about *where* the hands are and *what they do*.

**[Offensive holding](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-offensive-holding)** is a blocker grabbing,
hooking or tackling a defender, or restricting him with hands or arms outside his body's frame.
The rule's working idea is the **frame**: the body of the defender below the neck that faces the
blocker, in practice the chest plate between his shoulders. A blocker may put his hands inside the
frame and push, steer and lock on, and the rule tells him to work his hands there. What he may not do
is use his hands or arms to *materially restrict* the defender: grab and turn him, hook him, wrap him
up, take him to the ground. The test is the effect, not the hand position (a grab inside the frame
that jerks a rusher off his path is still holding), but most flagged holds are a hand outside the
frame (cloth at the shoulder, the side of the jersey, an arm). Officials also look at where it
happened: a hold away from the point of attack, or on a double team the defender didn't split, is
generally not called, because a defender who was never going to reach the play hasn't been robbed
of anything. The rule is aimed at holds that change the play. Holding costs **ten yards**: from the
previous spot on a pass, and on a run usually from the spot of the foul (the enforcement section
below explains why). If an offensive player holds in his own end zone, it is a **safety** (two points
and the ball to the other team): the spot the ten yards would be walked from is behind his own goal
line, and the rules don't move the ball around inside an end zone, they award the
points.[^holding-rule]

**[Illegal hands to the face](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-illegal-hands-to-the-face)** is the
foul for pushing, punching or grabbing an opponent's face mask, helmet or neck area with the hands.
The rule's test is **forcible** contact, **direct or prolonged**: a hand that slides up to the chin
and comes straight back down isn't called, while a palm that snaps a head back, or stays locked under
a face mask, is. That line decides whether an edge rusher's long-arm move becomes a flag. It goes
both ways: a lineman who snaps a pass rusher's head back with a palm to the face mask, or a
pass rusher who does the same to a blocker. The stat sheet files it as *illegal use of hands*, and
the price depends on who did it: **ten yards** against the offense, **five yards and an automatic
first down** against the defense.

### Why linemen hold, and why most holds aren't called

Pass protection is a losing fight by design. A pass rusher has to beat one man for a moment; a
blocker has to stay in front of him for two and a half seconds or more
([Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd)). When a rusher wins the edge,
the tackle's last resort is his hands, and a grab at the back of the jersey as the rusher turns the
corner is the hold you'll see flagged most often. From the lineman's side the trade is sometimes
worth it: a sack loses yards, a down and sometimes the ball, while a hold costs ten yards and replays
the down.

Officials could find a technical hold on most snaps, so the working standard is narrower: a grab
that materially restricts a defender, at or near the point of attack, especially one that turns
him, pulls him down or keeps him from the ball. That makes holding unusually sensitive to
instructions. In 2020 the league's officiating department told crews to call only "clear and
obvious" fouls rather than "ticky-tack stuff," and offensive holding flags fell from about 2.8 a game in 2019 to 1.8; they drifted back to about 2.5
by 2024 (the chart below shows it).[^holding2020]

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, holding is a slider: turn it up and the game calls more of it. In the
NFL, holding happens on most plays, in small ways, and the question is whether an official sees one
that matters. That makes holding calls lumpy: they cluster on edge rushers who win, on run plays at
the point of attack, and on crews and seasons with different standards. When the flag comes out, it
is usually because a defender was turned, pulled down or had a clear path to the ball taken away by
a hand outside the frame, not because a lineman touched a jersey.
:::

### Blocks that may not happen: in the back, low, and in pairs

Three more blocking rules shape how plays are drawn:

- **[Block in the back](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-block-in-the-back).** A block from behind,
  above the waist, on a player who is not the ball carrier. The NFL's name for it is an *illegal
  block above the waist*, and it costs **ten yards**, enforced from the spot of the foul. The same
  block *below* the waist is **clipping**, fifteen yards. It is the classic foul on kick returns and
  on screens, where blockers are running toward defenders who have already passed them. It is why
  return men and screen blockers are coached to "see the numbers, don't block them": if you can read
  the defender's jersey number on his back, let him go. One exception: in **close-line play**, the
  area around the line (roughly tackle to tackle, and up to three yards on the defense's side), a
  lineman may block a defender from behind above the waist. That's why a guard who catches a
  slanting tackle from behind on a down block isn't flagged.
- **Cut blocks, with limits.** A [cut block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cut-block) (at the
  thighs or below, from the front) is legal on a scrimmage down only near the ball: inside the *tight
  end box*, an area that runs from two yards outside each tackle and five yards either side of the
  line of scrimmage. Outside the box, low blocks are illegal (except against the ball carrier or a
  player trying to catch a pass), and so is any low block after a change of possession or on a kick.
  Even inside the box, a low block from behind or from the side while the blocker is moving back
  toward his own goal line (a *peel-back* block) has been illegal since 2013.[^lowblocks] The box
  rule doesn't care whether the play is a run or a pass, so cuts aren't only a zone-running tool: a
  running back may cut a blitzing linebacker inside the box to protect his quarterback, and some
  quick-game protections have linemen cut the rushers in front of them so the passer can see and
  throw over them.
- **[Chop block](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-chop-block).** Two blockers on the same defender,
  one high and one low at the thigh or below, together or in quick succession. The defender is held
  up by one and his legs taken out by the other, which is how knees get destroyed. The NFL narrowed
  the chop for years and banned it in **every situation in 2016**; it costs fifteen yards.

### The lineman's one-yard limit, enforced

The last blocking rule belongs to [Run-Pass Options](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd), which
explains it in full: on a pass, an ineligible lineman whose entire body is more than a yard past the
line when the ball is thrown is
[illegal man downfield](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-illegal-man-downfield), unless he got there
while still blocking a defender he engaged at the line. Its price is **five yards from the previous
spot**, with no loss of down, and a completed pass is wiped out. Note how that interacts with OPI.
A lineman who goes downfield and *blocks* a defender before the pass can be
flagged for pass interference instead (ten yards), and a receiver who blocks downfield before the
throw is OPI too. That is why NFL RPOs keep everyone's downfield blocking honest until the ball is
out.

**So how do screens work?** On a bubble or tunnel screen
([Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd))
receivers block cornerbacks and linemen lead the runner downfield, and it isn't a foul, because of
*timing*. In the NFL both rules apply to every forward pass, even one caught behind the line, and
both are about what happens **before the throw**. The OPI rule bans blocking more than a yard
downfield "clearly prior to a pass being thrown," so screen receivers are coached to get in the
defender's way without touching him and to start the block as the ball comes out. Linemen on a
screen engage a rusher at the line, let him go, and then slide sideways (or wait) until the throw:
the rule lets an ineligible player who made contact at the line drift past one yard as long as he
moves sideways or back, not upfield, until the ball is thrown. Then everyone turns upfield, and the
blocks that follow the catch are ordinary blocks, which is the situation in panel 3 of the figure
above.[^screens] (College is looser: its pass-interference rules cover only passes that cross the
neutral zone, and its linemen get three yards rather than one.)

In the data, ineligible-downfield flags rose as RPOs spread through the league, from about 0.06 a
game in 2015–2018 to 0.15–0.3 a game in most seasons since 2019 (2020, a light year for flags of
every kind, was the exception). The timing fits, though the data can't prove the RPO was the cause.

## Player safety: protecting the passer and the defenseless

The rules in this section are newer, mostly 21st century, and they exist for a different reason:
not to balance offense against defense but to keep players from being badly hurt, especially in the
head, neck and knees. They also cost the most. Almost all of them are **personal fouls**, the rule
book's category (Rule 12, Section 2) for contact that is dangerous or has no football purpose. A
personal foul costs **15 yards**, with an automatic first down when the defense commits it, and the
worst can bring an ejection, a fine or, from 2026, a suspension. An ejection (the rule book says
*disqualification*) is for a **flagrant** foul, which the rules define as one that is "extremely
objectionable, conspicuous, unnecessary, avoidable, or gratuitous"; the on-field officials make
that call, and since 2026 league officiating staff may consult on it from New York.[^flagrant]

### Roughing the passer

A quarterback in the act of throwing can't protect himself. His eyes are downfield, his arm is
cocked, his front leg is planted. **[Roughing the passer](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-roughing-the-passer)**
protects him in that posture and just after. The main ways to commit it:[^rtp]

- **Late.** Hitting him after the ball is clearly gone, once the defender has had a reasonable
  chance to stop (officials think in terms of a step or so).
- **High.** Forcible contact to his head or neck with the helmet, shoulder or forearm, even if the
  rusher was wrapping him up.
- **Low.** Forcible contact at or below the knees, unless the rusher was blocked into him. This is
  the "Brady rule," tightened in 2009 after Tom Brady tore knee ligaments on a low hit in the 2008
  season opener.
- **Heavy.** Landing on him with all or most of the defender's body weight, or driving him into the
  ground after the throw. It got a major emphasis in 2018, after Aaron Rodgers broke his collarbone
  when he was driven into the turf in 2017.
- **Stuffing him.** Picking him up and slamming him, or wrestling him down after the throw.

The price is **15 yards and an automatic first down**; if the pass is completed, the 15 yards are
walked off from the previous spot or the end of the play, whichever helps the offense more, so a
completion usually keeps its yards and gets the 15 on top. That makes roughing one of the most
expensive defensive fouls (see the chart in [What penalties cost](#what-penalties-cost)), and also one of the most
argued, because it asks an official to judge a 270-pound man's momentum in half a second. Two
roughing calls on consecutive days in October 2022, on Atlanta's Grady Jarrett for his sack of Tom
Brady and on Kansas City's Chris Jones for a strip-sack of Derek Carr, set off a week of debate about
whether the rule had gone too far.[^rtp2022]

The protection shrinks when the quarterback leaves the pocket. If he keeps moving or throws on the
run, he loses the one-step "late hit" protection and the protection against low hits, though the
head-and-neck and body-weight rules still apply. If he stops and sets up to throw again, he gets all
of it back.

### The sliding quarterback and the defenseless player

When a quarterback runs, he becomes a runner and can be tackled like one, with one exception. If
he **slides feet first**, he is giving himself up: the ball is dead the instant he touches the ground
with anything but his hands or feet, and defenders must treat him like a runner already
[down by contact](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-down-by-contact) (down because an opponent touched
him, the subject of the next chapter) and pull up. "Pull up" has a limit that decides most late-slide
arguments on a broadcast: a defender who had already committed to the tackle before the slide began
isn't flagged for contact he couldn't avoid, unless he hits the quarterback in the head or neck with
his helmet, shoulder or forearm, or does something else needlessly rough. The rule also puts the
burden on the quarterback: slide early, before a hit is imminent, or lose the protection. A
quarterback who *fakes* a slide is treated as having slid (the ball is dead
when he begins the fake), so he can't use it to freeze a defender and keep running. The current rule
treats a dive, feet or head first, the same way as a slide.[^slide]

The **[defenseless player](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-defenseless-player)** rule generalises
the idea. The rule book lists players who can't protect themselves: a passer in the act of throwing
or just after; a receiver trying to catch a pass (and until he has had time to protect himself after
the catch); a runner already held up with his
[forward progress](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-forward-progress) stopped (his advance halted, so
the play is effectively over); a kicker or punter during the
kick; a kick returner fielding the ball; a quarterback after a change of possession; a player on the
ground; a player hit by an illegal **blindside block** (a block thrown while the blocker is moving
toward or parallel to his own end line, with forcible contact from the helmet, forearm or shoulder;
itself 15 yards); a receiver running his route when the defender
comes from the side or behind; and a few others. Against them a
defender may not make forcible contact to the head or neck with the helmet, face mask, shoulder or
forearm, and may not **launch** (leave his feet and spring upward and forward into the player). The
foul is **[unnecessary roughness](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-unnecessary-roughness)**, the
catch-all personal foul that also covers late hits after the whistle and hits on players out of
bounds: **15 yards**, with an automatic first down when the defense commits it.[^defenseless]

The defenseless-player rule is why you see safeties aiming low, at a receiver's thighs, on a pass
over the middle instead of "lighting him up" high. It is a rule that changed how a position is played.

### The 2018 helmet rule

In 2018 the NFL went further with the **[use of the helmet (2018 rule)](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-use-of-the-helmet-2018-rule)**:
it is a foul for **any player, anywhere on the field**, to lower his head to initiate and make contact
with his helmet against an opponent. Unlike the defenseless-player rules, it covers runners and
blockers as well as tacklers, and it applies to everyone on every play, not just to hits on certain
players. The penalty is **15 yards**, and a flagrant violation can be an ejection.[^helmet]

### Tackles that are banned: the horse-collar and the hip-drop

Two tackles are illegal by name:

- **[Horse-collar tackle](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-horse-collar-tackle)** (banned in 2005).
  Grabbing the inside back or side collar of a runner's shoulder pads or jersey and pulling him down,
  usually from behind. The runner's legs fold under him as he falls backward, which breaks ankles and
  tears knee ligaments. The ban followed the 2004 season, in which Dallas safety Roy Williams's
  horse-collar tackles injured several players, among them Philadelphia's Terrell Owens.[^horsecollar]
  15 yards and an automatic first down.
- **[Hip-drop tackle](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hip-drop-tackle)** (banned in 2024). The
  tackler wraps the runner from behind or the side, swings his hips and legs off the ground, and drops
  his weight onto the runner's legs at or below the knee. The league's injury data showed the
  technique injuring runners at a far higher rate than ordinary tackles, and the owners banned it in
  March 2024, unanimously and over the objections of the players' union, with a 15-yard penalty and an automatic
  first down.[^hipdrop]

### Discipline beyond the flag: the 2026 three-strike policy

A flag is only one price. Players are also fined, and the worst hits bring suspensions. For the
2026 season the league and the players' union agreed on a **three-strike policy** for five listed
fouls (hip-drop tackles, horse-collar tackles, launching, hits on a defenseless player, and blindside
blocks): three violations bring a one-game suspension, and the strikes carry over into later seasons.
Everyone started the 2026 regular season with a clean slate. Reports differ on one detail: the
Associated Press describes three violations across the categories, while ProFootballTalk reads the
policy as three violations of the *same* rule. Strikes come from the league's discipline after
review, not only from flags.[^threestrike]
The point is to reach the habits that flags and fines hadn't changed, especially for the hip-drop,
which is rarely flagged (below).

| Rule | Since | What it bans | Price on the field | Why it was written |
|:--------------------|:------:|:----------------------|:--------------|:----------------------|
| Horse-collar tackle | 2005 | Pulling a runner down by the back or side collar | 15 yd + 1st down | Leg and ankle injuries from runners folded backward |
| Low hit on the passer ("Brady rule") | 2009 | Forcible hits at or below a passer's knees | 15 yd + 1st down | Knee injuries to quarterbacks |
| Chop block (all situations) | 2016 | High-low double blocks | 15 yd | Knee injuries to linemen |
| Use of the helmet | 2018 | Lowering the head to initiate helmet contact, anyone, anywhere | 15 yd, possible ejection | Head and neck injuries to both players |
| Roughing: body weight emphasis | 2018 | Landing on the passer with most of the body weight | 15 yd + 1st down | Shoulder and collarbone injuries to quarterbacks |
| Hip-drop tackle | 2024 | Swinging the hips onto a runner's legs | 15 yd + 1st down | Lower-leg injuries to runners |
| Three-strike policy | 2026 | Repeat violations of five listed safety rules | One-game suspension after three | Repeat offenders flags didn't deter |

: The main player-safety rules and when they arrived. Personal fouls by the defense carry an automatic first down; flagrant ones can bring an ejection. Sources in the footnotes to this section. {#tbl-safety}

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: safety rules with a scheme side effect"}
**What they solve.** Head, neck and knee injuries that a career, or a life, can't recover from.
**What they change.** Defensive backs tackle lower and play the ball instead of the man; rushers
learn to hit the quarterback's torso and roll off him; offenses gain yards on every borderline call,
and a quarterback who slides gets a free end to his run. Each rule also creates a judgment call, and
judgment calls on 15-yard fouls swing games. That tension, between protecting players and leaving
the officials too much to decide, runs through every live rules debate.
:::

## How a flag becomes yards: enforcement

Now the mechanics. When a flag flies during a play, the officials answer a fixed sequence of
questions. Learn them and you can usually announce the result before the referee does.

### Accept or decline

Most fouls happen during a live play, and the play keeps going until it ends normally. Then the team
that was fouled gets a choice: **[accept or decline](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-accept-decline-penalty)**.
Accept, and the result of the play is usually wiped out and the penalty enforced. Decline, and the
play stands as though no foul happened.[^enforce] In practice the head coach decides, quickly, with
the referee explaining the options to the team captain or the coach on the sideline.

The choice is usually obvious (nobody declines a 40-yard DPI) but not always:

- **Third down, incomplete pass, offensive holding.** Accept, and it's third-and-18 from ten yards
  back. Decline, and it's fourth-and-8: the offense will probably punt. Most defenses decline,
  because a stop now beats a long third down later. In 2021–2025 offenses converted third-and-16
  to third-and-20 about 10% of the time; a declined penalty that forces the
  punt takes even that chance away.
- **Defensive offside on a touchdown pass.** The offense declines and keeps the touchdown. A
  defensive *personal foul* on a touchdown isn't lost, though: the rules carry it over to the try,
  so the offense can kick the extra point from closer or go for two from the 1. (A personal foul on
  a successful extra-point kick can be carried to the kickoff instead.)
- **A sack and a hold.** If the offense held and the quarterback was sacked anyway for 9 yards, the
  defense can take the sack (and the down) or the 10 yards (and replay the down), whichever leaves
  the offense worse off.
- **Two fouls by the same team** on one play don't add up. The fouled team picks the one it wants
  enforced, and the other is dropped.
- **Fouls by both teams** on the same play usually **offset**: the penalties cancel and the down is
  replayed.

Some fouls aren't part of the choice in the usual way. Fouls *after* the play is over (a late hit, a
taunt, a fight) are **dead-ball fouls**: the play's result stands and the yardage is added on, from
where the play ended. That's how a 20-yard completion plus a late hit becomes 35 yards.[^td-fouls]

### Free plays

**[Free play](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-free-play)** is the accept-or-decline option seen
from the other end, and [The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) showed
it in action. When a defender is offside at the snap, the play goes on with the flag already down.
The offense can't lose: if the play works, it declines the penalty and keeps the result; if it fails
(incomplete, sacked, even intercepted), it takes the five yards. So quarterbacks are taught to snap
fast and take a shot downfield.

The catch is that not every jump gives a free play. If a defender's jump makes a nearby blocker
flinch, or leaves him with an unblocked path to the quarterback, the officials blow the whistle at
once: a **neutral zone infraction**, five yards, no play (encroachment if he touches someone). The
free play happens when the jumper draws no reaction and isn't running free, typically a wide end who
jumps and is picked up by his tackle, or a twelfth defender still running off the field at the snap
([What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)). That's also why the
quarterback snaps it *fast* on a jump: the play has to start before anybody reacts.[^nzi]

def free_play():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    dfn = defense("nickel", "single_high", off, press=True)
    dfn = [q.moved(label="C") if q.pos == "CB" else q for q in dfn]
    dfn = [q.moved(d=13.5, w=0.0) if q.key == "FS" else q.moved(d=2.5, w=-9.2) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    p.motion("WDE", to=(-0.2, -4.7), speed=2.4)                 # the jump: into the neutral zone
    p.route("X", r.go(32)); p.route("H", r.hitch(6)); p.route("Y", r.hitch(6)); p.route("Z", r.curl(12))
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.pass_to("X", t=1.7)
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
    for k in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.rush("WDE", pts=[(-1.6, 0.4)], speed=2.0)
    p.man("LCB", "X"); p.man("NB", "Y"); p.man("RCB", "Z"); p.man("SS", "H")
    p.drop("FS", (20.0, -6.0), speed=6.0)
    p.drop("MIKE", (6.0, 1.0)); p.drop("WILL", (6.0, -4.0))
    p.highlight("WDE", "X")
    return p

Snap: he has jumped into the neutral zone (dashed outline: where he was), but nobody flinched and the tackle is in front of him, so there is no whistle; the center snaps the ball before he can get back, he is offside, and the flag comes out while the play runs. The quarterback, knowing the offense can take five yards if this goes badly, throws deep to X against the press corner, a throw he would rarely risk on a normal second down. If X catches it, the offense declines the flag; if it falls incomplete or is intercepted, the offense accepts it and replays the down five yards closer. Had the tackle flinched, or had the end been running free at the quarterback, the officials would have blown it dead before the snap: a neutral zone infraction.

### From which spot, and how far

If the penalty is accepted, the officials need a starting point and a distance:

- **The previous spot** (where the ball was snapped) is the default for most fouls, including all
  pre-snap fouls, every foul during a pass play (offensive holding, offensive pass interference,
  defensive holding, illegal contact), and every offensive foul behind the line of scrimmage.
- **The spot of the foul** is used for defensive pass interference (the spot foul) and for many
  offensive fouls on running plays and returns: a block in the back 20 yards upfield on a punt
  return is walked off from where it happened.
- **The end of the play** is used for dead-ball fouls after the whistle, and is an option for a
  defensive personal foul such as roughing the passer on a completed pass (the offense gets
  whichever of the previous spot and the end of the play helps it more).

The middle bullet is the one fans get wrong, and it has a logic. On a run, the officials compare the
foul with the **end of the run**. A hold that happens *behind* that point, but past the line, is
walked off from the spot of the foul: the offense keeps the yards it gained up to the hold, which
came before the foul could help, and loses everything after it plus ten yards. A hold *beyond*
where the run ended couldn't have helped the runner, so it is walked off from the end of the run,
and the offense keeps the whole gain before paying ten yards. A hold behind the line of scrimmage
goes back to the previous spot, as on a pass.[^runenf] The NFL calls this the *three-and-one*
method; you only need the picture.

def yard_strip(ax, lo, hi, prev, half=6.75, num_w=-4.9):
    """A horizontal strip of field from yard line lo to hi (offense's own territory, moving right)."""
    los = 10 + prev
    f = Field(ax=ax, orient="horizontal", los=los, window=(10 + lo - los, 10 + hi - los),
              lateral=(FIELD_W / 2 - half, FIELD_W / 2 + half), to_go=None, numbers=False)
    p = Play([O_("Q", "QB", 0.0, 0.0, "")], [], los=los, ball_y=FIELD_W / 2, to_go=None)
    for yl in range(lo - lo % 10 + 10, hi, 10):
        say(f, p, yl - prev, num_w, str(yl) if yl else "G", color=style.MUTED, fs=7.5, weight="bold")
    return f, p


def run_row(ax, foul, end, new_spot, tag, note, from_spot):
    f, p = yard_strip(ax, 8, 56, 30, half=5.4, num_w=-3.8)

Then **how far**: five, ten or fifteen yards, or the spot. And then two adjustments near the goal
lines:

- **[Half the distance](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-half-the-distance).** A penalty may not
  move the ball more than halfway to the offending team's goal line. Holding by the offense on its
  own 8 moves the ball to the 4, not to the end zone. A defensive personal foul with the ball on the
  opponent's 6 moves it to the 3. Without the rule, a penalty could score points; with it, the ball
  keeps creeping toward the goal line but never gets there.[^halfdist]
- **Fouls in the end zone.** Offensive holding in the offense's own end zone is a **safety**: the
  spot the penalty would be walked from is already behind the goal line, so instead of moving the
  ball the rules give the defense two points. DPI in the end zone puts the ball on the 1, not in the
  end zone. The rule book awards a touchdown for a foul only in the rare case of a *palpably unfair
  act* (a player coming off the bench to tackle a runner headed for the end zone, say), and pass
  interference, however blatant, isn't one.[^palpably]

### What down is it?

Last question: the down.

- **Fouls by the offense** usually **replay the down**: second-and-10 becomes second-and-20 after a
  hold. A few also cost a down (an illegal forward pass, intentional grounding; see
  [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd)).
- **Fouls by the defense** come in two kinds. The pre-snap and procedural fouls (offside,
  encroachment, neutral zone infraction, too many men) replay the down unless the yards reach the line
  to gain. The contact and safety fouls (defensive holding, illegal contact, DPI, roughing the passer,
  unnecessary roughness and the other personal fouls, illegal hands to the face) carry an
  **automatic first down**, however short the yardage.
- **A half can't end on an accepted defensive foul during a play.** If time runs out on a play
  with a defensive foul and the offense accepts, it gets one untimed down.

::: {#cell-fig-flag-flow .cell execution_count=13}

includes the play the flag wiped out, which is gone; the EPA reflects only where the penalty left the
ball.) Averaging by foul type gives a price list in points.

Four things stand out.

1. **The automatic first down is worth more than the yards.** Defensive holding and illegal contact
   are five-yard fouls, the same yardage as a false start, yet they swing about a point toward the
   offense while a false start costs about two-thirds of one the other way. Splitting the two-sided
   fouls by team shows the same thing: hands to the face is worth more against the defense (five
   yards and a first down) than offside is (five yards, no first down).
2. **DPI and roughing the passer cost a defense more than a completed pass usually gains.** The
   average completion in these seasons was worth about \+0\.80 EPA; a DPI flag
   averaged \+1\.74, and roughing
   \+1\.76.
3. **Offensive holding is a drive-killer.** At about \-1\.00
   EPA, a hold costs a little over half of what a sack does (\-1\.78 on average), and
   holds are flagged about two and a half times a game.
4. **The same five-yard foul is worth more on later downs.** The table shows it.

On first-and-10 a defensive hold is a modest gain, first-and-5. On third-and-7 it erases a likely
punt and hands the offense a fresh set of downs, so it's worth about three times as much. That's why
defensive coordinators preach discipline on third down above all, and why an offense with a long
third down will often throw toward the corner it thinks is most likely to grab.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: penalties in EPA work"}
Analysts don't agree on how to treat penalty snaps. The usual "EPA per play" leaves out snaps that a
penalty wiped out (nflverse marks them `play_type == "no_play"`), which drops most DPI flags and most
holding calls from team numbers. [Expected Points and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd)
shows how much that choice shades run-versus-pass comparisons; the DPI flags alone make passing look
a little better once they are counted. For your own work: say which choice you made, and remember
that nflverse records one foul per play, so a play with two flags carries only one penalty type.

Labels move, too. The 2018 helmet foul appears in nflverse under its own name, "lowering the head
to initiate contact," at about 0.07 to 0.13 flags a game from 2018 to 2020, then fades in 2021 and
vanishes from the labels after that.[^helmet-data] Whether those calls dried up or are now filed
under another name (unnecessary roughness is the likely home), the series breaks there. Check a
category's history before you chart it.
:::

## The rules keep moving: live debates

Every spring the competition committee and the teams propose rule changes, and the owners vote; a
change needs 24 of 32 votes. The rules in this chapter will keep changing, so here are the debates
that were live going into the 2026 season. (For how these fit the long history of rule changes,
see [The 1978 Liberation](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd) and
[Dynasties and Counterpunches](../11-history/11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd); for the
timeline, [Appendix E](../../appendices/appendix-e-rules-timeline-trees.qmd).)

- **The tush push.** The [tush push](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tush-push) is a quarterback
  sneak with teammates shoving the quarterback from behind, the Eagles' near-automatic short-yardage
  play ([Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd)
  explains it). Pushing the runner has been legal since the NFL removed its ban in 2005; *pulling*
  him (a teammate grabbing his arm or jersey and hauling him forward) is still a foul, ten yards, and
  it's the one to watch for in a tush-push pile. In 2025 Green
  Bay proposed banning it again; the proposal was tabled in the spring and a revised version **failed
  22–10 on May 21, 2025**, two votes short of 24. The league tightened its officiating guidance on false
  starts and alignment instead. For 2026, **no team proposed a ban**, and the play is legal this
  season.[^tush] The argument is about safety (a pile of linemen driving forward), about fairness (is
  a nearly unstoppable play bad for the game?) and about whether one team's mastery of a play is a
  reason to outlaw it. The case study is
  [The Eagles: Trenches, RPOs, and the Tush Push](../12-case-studies/12-06-eagles-trenches-and-tush-push.qmd).
- **Is the hip-drop ban being enforced?** The tackle was banned in 2024, but on-field flags have been
  extremely rare: nflverse's play-by-play records 1 hip-drop flag
  in the 2024 regular season and 2 in 2025. The technique happens
  in a blur, from behind, in a pile, which is hard for an official to see live. The league has
  leaned on fines after the game instead, and the 2026 three-strike policy adds suspensions on top.
  Whether discipline after the fact changes behaviour as much as flags would is the open question.
- **Replay for judgment calls.** After the 2019 pass-interference experiment failed, the NFL moved
  more carefully. Since 2025 replay assist may help the referee on objective facts and may
  **overturn** flags for hits on a defenseless player, face mask (grabbing and twisting or pulling
  the face mask), horse-collar, tripping (using a leg to trip an opponent) and roughing or running
  into the kicker (hitting a punter or kicker after the kick). It **cannot add** a foul that wasn't called, and roughing the passer and
  pass interference are not on the list. In 2026 league officials may also be consulted on ejections
  for flagrant acts.[^replay] Proposals for a full "sky judge" who could call fouls from the booth
  keep coming back.
- **College versus NFL.** The college game caps DPI at 15 yards, gives linemen three yards
  downfield instead of one, and treats targeting (a forcible hit to the head) with automatic
  ejections. College offensive pass interference was cut from 15 yards to 10 for 2026.[^ncaa2026]
  Each difference is a live argument for moving the NFL rule toward college, or the reverse; the full
  side-by-side table is in [Appendix E](../../appendices/appendix-e-rules-timeline-trees.qmd) and the
  history in [The College Laboratory](../11-history/11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the flag predictor"}
Every time a yellow flag flies, play referee before the referee does. Say your answers out loud,
then check them against the announcement.

- **Where did the flag come from?** The official's position is a clue. A flag from deep
  downfield (the side judges, field judge or back judge) is usually pass interference, illegal
  contact or defensive holding. A flag from the officials at the line of scrimmage or behind the
  offense is usually holding, a false start or a foul on the quarterback. A flag thrown late, after
  the play, is usually a personal foul. (Who stands where is in
  [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd).)
- **Was the ball in the air?** If a receiver was grabbed before the throw, guess holding or illegal
  contact (five yards, first down). After the throw, guess DPI and estimate the spot.
- **Accept or decline?** Ask what the fouled team gave up on the play, and whether the next down
  (a punt down, say) already punishes the offense more than the yards would.
- **Enforce it.** Which spot, how far, half the distance near a goal line, and what down. Say the new
  down and distance.
- **Free play?** If a defender jumped and the ball was snapped anyway, watch the quarterback take
  his shot.
- **Keep score.** By the end of a game you'll be calling most flags right. For a running tally,
  log the penalties' expected-points cost from the chart in
  [What penalties cost](#what-penalties-cost): which team gave away more points in flags?
:::
